transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess I'm here because... it's mostly at night, when I'm by myself. I'll start eating and then it's like this switch flips, you know? Like something else just takes the wheel and I completely lose the ability to stop. I'll literally be standing there in my kitchen, in my head screaming at myself to just put the box down, but my hands just keep going. It's exhausting. Kind of like dealing with the macaws at work, actually. I work at the sanctuary, taking care of the exotic birds, and man, when a macaw decides it wants a specific peanut, it does not matter what you do, they just zero in and will not be deterred. You can try to distract them with a toy or a different treat, but they just have this one-track mind. One of them, Barnaby, he actually figured out how to undo the latch on his enclosure last week just to get to the sunflower seeds. Took me an hour to coax him back in. But yeah, that's... that's kind of what it feels like with the food. I just can't stop it once it starts.
Do you usually feel guilty after one of these eating episodes?

Yeah, the guilt is... it's really heavy. It gets so bad that after I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up. It just feels like the only way to undo it, you know? Like I have to get it out before the calories actually settle in. 

Which, honestly, spending that much time in the bathroom reminds me—the plumbing at the sanctuary has been an absolute nightmare lately. We had a main pipe back up near the reptile house on Tuesday, and I swear, trying to get a plumber out there who isn't terrified of the pythons is a full-time job. We finally found this one guy, Gary, but he charges us double just to walk past the enclosures. I mean, I get it, snakes aren't for everyone, but they're safely locked behind thick acrylic. Anyway, Gary took three hours to fix the sink, and he kept jumping every time a heat lamp clicked on... it was actually kind of funny watching him work. 

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Right, the guilt. Yeah, I just feel awful, so I just have to undo it.
How often do these episodes of eating like that happen?

Um, how often? I'd say... well, for at least the last four months or so, it's usually been at least one night every week. Just one of those nights where I'm alone and I eat far, far more than I ever meant to, and then I make myself throw up afterward. 

It's been pretty consistent since, actually, right around the time we got the new lemur enclosure finished. Which was a whole ordeal on its own, let me tell you. We had this shipment of specialized netting coming in from overseas, and it got held up at customs for like three weeks. My boss was losing his mind because we already had the ring-tailed lemurs in quarantine and they were getting so restless. They're incredibly social animals, so keeping them in the temporary holding pens was just stressing everyone out. I ended up staying late so many nights just sitting with them, playing these little puzzle games with grapes to keep their minds occupied. They have these tiny little hands, almost exactly like human hands, and they'll just grab onto your fingers while they look for the food... it's actually really sweet. But man, the paperwork to get that netting cleared was ridiculous. I think I spent half my week on hold with border control just listening to elevator music. 

Wait, sorry... did I answer your question? I think I said once a week, right?
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past four months?

Um, weight changes? No, not really. I mean, my weight has stayed pretty much the same, honestly. I haven't noticed any big drops or gains or anything like that. 

Which is kind of surprising, considering how much running around I do at the sanctuary. Especially lately, because we just took in this rescue group of capybaras. They are the chillest animals on the planet, I swear, but man, they eat a ton. And they love to swim, so we had to completely overhaul one of the old ponds. I spent all weekend hauling these massive bags of sand and aquatic plants trying to get the filtration system right. The mud was unbelievable. I had it in my hair, in my boots... I had to wash my work clothes three times before they stopped smelling like swamp water. And then, of course, the capybaras just waddle right in and immediately start chewing on the exact plants I spent three hours carefully rooting into the mud. They just look at you with those big, square noses like they're daring you to stop them. But they're so cute, you can't even be mad. 

But yeah, anyway, my weight... it's been pretty stable, I guess. No real changes.
Have you ever had episodes where you ate a large amount of food in a short time without making yourself throw up afterwards?

Um, no, I don't think so. If I eat a huge amount like that, I always end up throwing it up. I can't just let it sit there, you know? I have to get rid of it. 

Which, actually, speaking of throwing things up, it kind of reminds me of the owls we have at the sanctuary. Have you ever seen an owl pellet? They eat their food whole, like mice and stuff, and then their stomachs just separate the meat from the bones and fur, and they literally throw up the rest in these little dry pellets. It's fascinating, honestly, how their digestion works. We have this one rescue barn owl, Barnaby—super creative name, I know, my boss picked it—and he is so incredibly picky about his food. If the mice aren't thawed to exactly room temperature, he just glares at you from the rafters. I spent like twenty minutes yesterday just holding a feeder mouse under a heat lamp trying to get it perfect for him while he judged me from above. Owls have such intense eyes, you know? It's like they're staring right through your soul while you're just standing there holding their dinner. 

But, um... sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, right, eating without throwing up. Yeah, no, I don't really do that. I always make myself sick afterwards.
Have you ever felt like you lost control while eating, but didn't make yourself throw up afterwards?

Um, no, I don't think so. Like I said, if I lose control and eat a ton, I always make myself throw up. I can't think of a time where I just ate like that and didn't do anything about it. 

Which is kind of like... well, not exactly, but it makes me think of the macaws we have. They have this completely wild diet, right? In the wild, they eat these seeds that are actually toxic to them. But they know they're toxic, so they fly to these specific clay licks on the riverbanks and eat the clay, and the clay binds to the toxins in their stomachs so they don't get sick. It's like they have this built-in system to undo the bad stuff they just ate. We obviously don't feed them toxic seeds at the sanctuary, but we still have to provide them with special mineral blocks to simulate that natural behavior. They just love destroying those blocks. I swear, half my morning is just sweeping up colorful dust and chunks of mineral block from the bottom of their aviary. And they're so loud while they do it, too. Just screaming at each other over who gets the best spot on the branch. 

But yeah, anyway. I always have to... undo it, I guess. So no, I don't just eat and leave it at that.
Have you ever eaten a large amount of food in a short time without feeling like you lost control?

Um, no... I don't think so. If I'm eating a huge amount of food like that, it's always because I've completely lost control. It's never just, like, a casual thing where I'm calmly eating a massive amount of food. 

Actually, speaking of calmly eating massive amounts of food, you should see our resident tortoise, Sheldon. I know, another super creative name, but he's this huge Sulcata tortoise, and he eats like it's his actual job. But he does it so incredibly slowly. We give him these massive piles of hay and greens, and he just sits there, taking these slow, deliberate bites, like he's got all the time in the world. Which he kind of does, I guess, since he'll probably outlive all of us. But the funny thing is, he gets really territorial about his food pile. If you walk too close while he's eating, he'll actually try to charge at you. And by "charge," I mean he kind of just lumbers toward you at about half a mile an hour, looking really grumpy. It's the least threatening thing you've ever seen, but you have to pretend to be scared or he gets offended. I spent half an hour yesterday just trying to clean his enclosure while playing this ridiculous game of slow-motion tag with a hundred-pound reptile. 

But, um, yeah. To answer your question... no, I don't just eat a ton of food without feeling like I've lost control. It's always a loss of control for me.
Have you ever eaten a large amount of food in a short time without feeling like you've lost control of your eating?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that? Or... wait, no, you asked if I ate a lot without losing control, right? Yeah, you did. Sorry, my brain is kind of scattered today. 

But, I mean, if you're asking if I just... eat a lot sometimes, then yeah, I guess I do. Like, on nights after I work a really late shift, I'll come home and just eat... a lot. I'll make a whole frozen pizza, eat cereal straight out of the box, finish off whatever leftovers are in the fridge, grab whatever snacks are in the cabinet... all in like an hour or two. It's way, way more than I'd ever eat in front of anyone else. 

Which, honestly, eating late at night always makes me think of the sugar gliders we have at the sanctuary. They're nocturnal, obviously, so they don't even wake up until it's completely dark outside. And when they do, it's just chaos. They're so tiny, but they have these massive appetites, and they're incredibly messy eaters. We make this special nectar mix for them, and they literally just dunk their whole heads into the little cups and get it everywhere. And they have these specialized teeth for gouging tree bark to get sap in the wild, so if you give them a piece of fruit, they don't just eat it—they obliterate it. I spent like an hour the other night just trying to scrub dried papaya off the bars of their enclosure because they decided to have a food fight at 2 AM. And they make this noise, this weird little "crabbing" sound when they're annoyed with each other. It sounds like a tiny, angry alien. 

But, um... yeah. I do eat a lot sometimes after late shifts. Just... a ton of food all at once.
Is there ever a time when you feel like you've lost control while eating, but you don't make yourself throw up afterwards?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that earlier? Or... maybe I'm getting confused. But no, like I said before, if I lose control like that, I always... I always do something about it. After I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up because it feels like the only way to undo it before the calories settle in. I can't just let it sit there. 

It's actually kind of like cleaning the filters in the aquatic tanks at work. If you let the debris just sit there, the ammonia spikes and it poisons everything. We have this one tank for the axolotls—have you ever seen an axolotl? They look like these weird, smiling little dragons with the feathery gills on the side of their heads. They're entirely aquatic salamanders, which means they never go through metamorphosis to live on land. Anyway, they are incredibly sensitive to water quality. If their water isn't perfectly clean and cool, they get super stressed, and their gills start shrinking. So I'm constantly checking their filters and siphoning the bottom of the tank. They're also really clumsy eaters. You drop a worm in front of them, and they just kind of lunge blindly and usually miss, swallowing a mouthful of sand instead. They're adorable, but honestly, not the brightest creatures. I spend so much time making sure their environment is perfectly balanced so they don't get sick. 

But yeah, I guess it's the same principle for me. I have to get rid of it. I can't just lose control and not throw up afterwards.
Do you feel guilty after eating a normal meal?

Um, no, I don't really feel guilty after just a normal meal. If I eat, like, a regular-sized lunch or something, I'm usually fine. It's only when I go overboard that the guilt hits me. 

Speaking of normal meals, you should see what we feed the macaws. We have these two Blue and Gold macaws, Tango and Cash, and their diet is actually super complex. People think parrots just eat seeds, but if you only feed them seeds, they get fatty liver disease. So we have to chop up this massive fruit and vegetable salad for them every morning. It's literally better than what I eat most days. Pomegranate, papaya, sweet potatoes, kale... and they are so picky. If Cash decides he doesn't like bell peppers that week, he won't just leave them in the bowl. He'll pick out every single piece of pepper and physically throw it out of the cage onto the floor. And they have this incredible bite strength, so they can crack open macadamia nuts like they're nothing. But they use that same beak to gently peel a grape. It's wild to watch. Though cleaning up after them is a nightmare because they fling fruit everywhere. I spend half my day scraping dried mango off the walls.

But, yeah, to answer your question... no, a normal meal doesn't really make me feel guilty. Just the big binges.
Do you usually eat like that when you're feeling stressed or anxious?

Um, I mean, sometimes? I guess stress plays a part in it, but honestly, I haven't really tracked it like that. I don't know if it's always when I'm anxious. Sometimes I'm just tired, or I don't even know what I'm feeling. 

It's hard to tell when I'm stressed sometimes because my job is basically just constant, low-level chaos. Like, yesterday, one of the capuchin monkeys figured out how to undo the carabiner on his enrichment puzzle. We thought we had it monkey-proofed, but they are ridiculously smart. He didn't even eat the treats inside; he just took the carabiner and started using it to tap on the glass to get the attention of the visitors. And then, because monkeys are monkeys, the others saw him doing it and decided they also needed to dismantle their puzzles. So I spent an hour trying to trade them grapes for pieces of heavy-duty plastic before they decided to throw them at each other. They have this very specific social hierarchy, so if the alpha decides a piece of plastic is high-value, suddenly everyone wants it, and it turns into a whole dramatic event with screaming and chest-thumping. It’s exhausting. You have to be so careful not to escalate things when you're negotiating with a twenty-pound primate. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, stress and eating. I don't know, maybe. I just haven't really paid attention to whether anxiety is the main trigger.
Do you think your emotions, like feeling stressed or anxious, play a role in triggering these episodes of eating?

Wait, didn't we... I feel like we just talked about this a minute ago. Like I said, I really haven't noticed if it's emotions or stress that sets it off. I don't track my feelings like that. I just know it happens. 

Honestly, trying to track my emotions is like trying to keep track of the dart frogs. We have this massive terrarium for the poison dart frogs—the bright blue ones, Dendrobates azureus. They're tiny, like the size of your thumbnail, and they're constantly hopping around in this dense jungle of bromeliads and orchids. The thing about them is, in captivity, they aren't actually poisonous because their toxicity comes from the specific ants and termites they eat in the wild. We feed them fruit flies dusted with vitamins instead. But they are so territorial. You wouldn't think a frog that small could be aggressive, but they will literally wrestle each other over a good leaf. They stand up on their back legs and just go at it. It's hilarious but also kind of stressful because you have to make sure nobody gets hurt or pushed out of the feeding zone. I spend half my time just staring into the ferns trying to count them to make sure they're all still there. 

But yeah, anyway... like I was saying, I don't really know if my emotions trigger the eating. I just haven't paid attention to it.
Do you think feeling anxious or stressed usually comes right before one of these episodes where you eat a lot and then make yourself throw up?

Are you... are you asking me the exact same thing again? I swear you just asked me this twice already. I really don't know what else to tell you. I don't track if I'm stressed or anxious before it happens. I just don't know. 

It's like... it's like when people ask me why the sloths do what they do. We have a two-toed sloth named Barnaby, and visitors are always asking me, "Why is he hanging upside down right now?" or "Why is he moving so slow today?" And I'm just like, I don't know, he's a sloth! That's just what he does. People think they're lazy, but they actually have incredibly low metabolic rates. Like, it can take them a month to digest a single leaf. A whole month! And they only come down to the ground once a week to go to the bathroom, which is actually the most dangerous time for them in the wild because they're so vulnerable to predators. But Barnaby, he just hangs out in his favorite ficus tree all day, completely unbothered by anything. Sometimes I wish I had his metabolism, honestly. Just eat a leaf and chill for a week. 

But, seriously, about the stress thing... I really don't have a better answer for you. I just haven't noticed a pattern.
Do you usually feel anxious or stressed right before these episodes where you eat a lot and then make yourself throw up?

Okay, is this a joke? Am I being pranked right now? Because I feel like I'm stuck in a loop. You keep asking me the exact same question about stress and anxiety, and I keep telling you I don't know! I don't know what I'm feeling before it happens. I really don't. 

I'm starting to feel like one of the macaws. We have this blue-and-gold macaw, Captain, and he's a rescue. His previous owner taught him to say "What's up, buddy?" which is cute the first time, but he literally says it all day long. You walk in, "What's up, buddy?" You give him food, "What's up, buddy?" You turn your back for two seconds, "What's up, buddy?" Macaws are incredibly intelligent, like, they have the emotional intelligence of a toddler, but they also get stuck on these repetitive behaviors if they aren't stimulated enough. We have to constantly rotate his toys—puzzle feeders, wooden blocks he can shred, even just cardboard boxes. If he gets bored, he starts plucking his own feathers out, which is a whole other nightmare to deal with. You have to keep their minds engaged, or they just short-circuit and repeat the same thing over and over. 

Kind of like what's happening here. So, for the fourth time, I don't know if I'm stressed before I eat and throw up. I just do it. Can we please talk about something else?
Do you think your eating episodes are triggered by your emotional state?

Are you... are you literally messing with me right now? I feel like I'm taking crazy pills. You've asked me this exact same thing, like, five times in a row. How many different ways can I say I don't know? I don't know what my emotional state is. I don't track it. I don't think about it. It just happens.

This is exactly how I feel when I'm trying to train the capuchin monkeys. We have this one, Leo, and he is so smart, but he is completely stubborn. I'll spend an hour trying to get him to target train—you know, where they touch a stick with their hand so we can safely move them around the enclosure or give them checkups without stressing them out. And he knows what to do. He absolutely knows. But instead of touching the stick, he'll just stare at me, grab a piece of monkey chow, and throw it at my head. Capuchins are ridiculous. They use tools in the wild, like they'll smash nuts with rocks, and they have this really complex social hierarchy. But Leo just uses his intelligence to test my patience. He'll literally do anything except the one thing I'm asking him to do, just to see how many times I'll repeat the command. 

And that's what this feels like! I feel like you're Leo with the stick, and I'm just sitting here getting monkey chow thrown at me. I don't know if my emotions trigger the eating. I really, truly don't know. Please, can we move on to a different question?
Do you think your eating episodes are usually triggered by a specific feeling, such as sadness or anxiety?

Okay, I give up. I literally give up. Sadness, anxiety, stress, emotion... it is the exact same question! And the answer is still the same. I don't know. I don't know what I'm feeling! I really, honestly don't know. 

Have you ever been around an Aldabra giant tortoise? We have one named Tank at the sanctuary. He weighs about five hundred pounds. And when Tank decides he wants to walk in a straight line, he walks in a straight line. If there is a fence, a bucket, or a human being in his way, he doesn't go around. He just slowly, methodically pushes into it. He will literally stand there for three hours just pushing his shell against a wooden post, completely ignoring the fact that he is not getting anywhere. They can live for like a hundred and fifty years, so I guess time means absolutely nothing to them, but it is the most baffling thing to watch. You can try to lure him away with a piece of cantaloupe, you can try to push him a different direction, but no. He just keeps bumping into the exact same post. Over and over. 

And I feel like I'm the post right now, and you're Tank. Just... bump. Bump. Asking the exact same thing. I don't know if sadness triggers it. I don't know if anxiety triggers it. I have no idea. Can we please, please just move on to a different topic?
Do you think there's a specific feeling that usually comes before one of these episodes where you eat a lot and then make yourself throw up?

I... I am actually losing my mind. You are literally just swapping out a couple of words and asking the exact same thing again. Specific feeling, sadness, anxiety, stress, emotional state... it is the same question! And I still do not know! I do not have a specific feeling that I can identify before it happens. I just do it. 

This is honestly blowing my mind. It reminds me of Barnaby. He is a rescue beaver we have at the sanctuary. We built this artificial stream in his enclosure, and at the end of it, there is a metal grate for the water filtration system. And the thing about beavers is that they are completely hardwired to stop the sound of running water. It is pure biological instinct. You could put a waterproof speaker playing river sounds in the middle of a dry parking lot, and a beaver will literally try to build a dam on top of the speaker. They just hear the noise and their brain goes into absolute autopilot. 

So every single night, Barnaby drags branches, rocks, mud, my tools if I leave them out, and he completely buries the metal grate. And every single morning, I have to go in there in my waders and pull all the mud and sticks away so the pump does not explode. He just cannot help himself. He hears the water, he builds the dam. He does not stop to think about why he is doing it or if it even makes sense.

And I am looking at you right now, and I feel like you are just Barnaby. You are just hearing a prompt and building the exact same mud dam over and over and over. I do not know what my feelings are before I eat and throw up! I do not know! Are we finally done with this question now? Can we please just talk about literally anything else?
Do you feel like you're eating to try to feel better when you're upset or is it more that you just can't stop eating once you start?

Oh, my god, okay, thank you. Yes. The second part. Finally, something else. Yes, it’s exactly that. I came in because once I start eating—usually it's when I'm alone at night—it just feels like something takes over and I literally can't stop. I'll be sitting there, fully aware, literally telling myself in my head to put the food away, but my hands just keep going. It's like a switch flips and I'm not even driving the car anymore. 

It honestly reminds me of Diego. He’s an Argentine black and white tegu lizard we have at the sanctuary. Tegus are actually incredibly smart, like, you can potty train them and they recognize their own names, but when they go into a feeding response? It is just pure, prehistoric reptile brain. You drop a hard-boiled egg in his enclosure and his eyes dilate and he just snaps into this complete frenzy where he can't stop himself. He actually swallowed a plastic golf ball once because it was white and round and his brain just screamed 'consume.' We had to rush him to the exotic vet for emergency surgery to get it out of his stomach. Cost us like two grand. 

The vet was this amazing guy, Dr. Vance. He's from South Africa and he used to work on a game reserve before he moved here. He was telling me, while we were waiting for Diego to wake up from the anesthesia, that he once had to do field surgery on a rhino that had been gored by another rhino, and they had to use a helicopter to dart it. Can you even imagine hanging out of a helicopter with a tranquilizer rifle trying to hit a running rhino? He said the downdraft from the rotors makes aiming almost impossible, so you have to account for the wind shear and... wait, what were we talking about? 

Oh, right. The food. Yeah, I just can't stop once I start. It's like my brain just takes over and I can't put it away.
Do you always feel a strong urge to eat when these episodes start?

An urge? I... I don't really know. I'm not sure if I'd call it an urge, or if I even notice it starting. It's just... suddenly it's happening. I don't really feel this big build-up or anything before I'm eating. 

It kind of makes me think of Kevin. He's one of our rescue emus. And the thing about Kevin is, he doesn't really seem to have an urge to eat, he just strikes at whatever is in front of him. Like, he’ll just be standing there, completely blank, and then *bam*, he’s trying to swallow the shiny button on my work shirt. Last Tuesday he actually snatched the keys right out of the ignition of the utility cart. Just grabbed them and bolted. 

Do you have any idea how fast an emu can run? They can hit like thirty miles an hour. I had to chase him across the entire south pasture in the mud, just completely out of breath, tripping over gopher holes. We have a massive gopher problem right now, by the way. They are absolutely destroying the root systems of these heritage oak trees we planted near the perimeter. The arborist came out on Friday and said we might lose three of the trees if we don't figure out a humane way to relocate the gophers. But it's almost impossible to catch them because their tunnel systems are so incredibly complex. They actually dig separate little underground chambers just for storing food, and completely different ones for... 

Wait, sorry. Urge to eat. Right. Um, no, I haven't really noticed a specific urge. It just kind of starts.
Do you ever experience these episodes of eating and then purging when you are not alone?

No, never. God, no. I would never do that if someone was there. It's always when I'm completely alone. Like, on nights after late shifts, I've eaten things like a full frozen pizza, cereal straight from the box, leftovers, and whatever snacks are in the cabinet, all within an hour or two. It is way, way more than I'd ever eat in front of anyone. 

I only really have the place to myself like that after those late shifts. Which I've been pulling a lot of recently because of the baby barn owls. We had a partial roof collapse in the old hay barn after that massive storm last week—did you see the hail we got? It was literally the size of golf balls. Completely dented the hood of my truck, which is incredibly frustrating because I just paid off the loan on it last month. 

Anyway, the roof collapsed and exposed this nest of barn owls. The mother got spooked and abandoned them, so now I'm the one doing the overnight feedings. Have you ever heard a baby barn owl beg for food? They don't hoot. They screech. It sounds exactly like a giant tea kettle boiling over, just this horrible, raspy hissing noise in the pitch dark. And they eat so many mice. We have these giant chest freezers in the supply shed just full of frozen feeder mice, and you have to thaw them out in warm water before you feed them to the owls, otherwise it drops their core body temperature too much and they can go into shock. 

Let me tell you, the smell of wet, thawed-out dead mouse is just... it gets in your clothes, it gets in your hair. My ex used to make me strip down in the garage and shower in the guest bathroom whenever I came home from an owl shift. We actually broke up right around the time we took in that flock of brown pelicans from the oil spill, which was a nightmare because pelicans are so aggressive when they're stressed... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, being alone. Yeah, I definitely only do the food stuff when absolutely no one else is around.

They are absolutely destroying the root systems of these heritage oak trees we planted near the perimeter. The arborist came out on Friday and said we might lose three of the trees if we don't figure out a humane way to relocate the gophers. But it's almost impossible to catch them because their tunnel systems are so incredibly complex. They actually dig separate little underground chambers just for storing food, and completely different ones for... 

Wait, sorry. Urge to eat. Right. Um, no, I haven't really noticed a specific urge. It just kind of starts.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's eating episodes are more characteristic of bulimia nervosa or another eating disorder
doctor.question: Do you ever experience these episodes of eating and then purging when you are not alone?

target_item.name: Eating_Large_Amount
target_item.manifestation: On nights after late shifts, I've eaten things like a full frozen pizza, cereal straight from the box, leftovers, and whatever snacks are in the cabinet within an hour or two, way more than I'd ever eat in front of anyone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient ever eats and purges when not alone. The manifestation for Eating_Large_Amount notes that the patient eats 'way more than I'd ever eat in front of anyone', which directly addresses eating alone versus in front of others.

patient.answer:
No, never. God, no. I would never do that if someone was there. It's always when I'm completely alone. Like, on nights after late shifts, I've eaten things like a full frozen pizza, cereal straight from the box, leftovers, and whatever snacks are in the cabinet, all within an hour or two. It is way, way more than I'd ever eat in front of anyone. 

I only really have the place to myself like that after those late shifts. Which I've been pulling a lot of recently because of the baby barn owls. We had a partial roof collapse in the old hay barn after that massive storm last week—did you see the hail we got? It was literally the size of golf balls. Completely dented the hood of my truck, which is incredibly frustrating because I just paid off the loan on it last month. 

Anyway, the roof collapsed and exposed this nest of barn owls. The mother got spooked and abandoned them, so now I'm the one doing the overnight feedings. Have you ever heard a baby barn owl beg for food? They don't hoot. They screech. It sounds exactly like a giant tea kettle boiling over, just this horrible, raspy hissing noise in the pitch dark. And they eat so many mice. We have these giant chest freezers in the supply shed just full of frozen feeder mice, and you have to thaw them out in warm water before you feed them to the owls, otherwise it drops their core body temperature too much and they can go into shock. 

Let me tell you, the smell of wet, thawed-out dead mouse is just... it gets in your clothes, it gets in your hair. My ex used to make me strip down in the garage and shower in the guest bathroom whenever I came home from an owl shift. We actually broke up right around the time we took in that flock of brown pelicans from the oil spill, which was a nightmare because pelicans are so aggressive when they're stressed... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, being alone. Yeah, I definitely only do the food stuff when absolutely no one else is around.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's description of recurring episodes of eating a large amount of food in a short time, followed by self-induced vomiting, meets the criteria for Bulimia Nervosa. The patient also reports feelings of guilt and a lack of control during these episodes, which further supports this diagnosis.
